title: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
summary: Compress embeddings to one bit per dimension: sign bits with Hamming distance and rescoring, RaBitQ's rotation, unbiased estimator and bound, its use in IVF and graphs, multi-bit codes and a Faiss lab.
outcomes: Compute a binary code, its Hamming distance and the sign dot product D - 2H for a small vector pair
Explain why oversampling plus rescoring recovers recall, and why sign bits fail on non-centered data
Trace RaBitQ encoding: centering, random rotation, sign bits and the stored <o-bar,o> factor
Compute RaBitQ's unbiased estimate and explain why its error shrinks as 1/sqrt(D)
Explain per-cluster query re-centering in IVF-RaBitQ and why libraries use O(D log D) rotations
Find an extended RaBitQ code by enumerating critical rescaling values, and compare it with scalar quantization
Benchmark RaBitQ against plain BQ, PQ and int8 in Faiss at matched bytes, with sanity checks
Choose between plain BQ, BBQ, RaBitQ, extended RaBitQ and int8 given memory, recall and rescoring limits

lessons.title: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension

blocks.md: In product quantization you compressed vectors by splitting them into sub-vectors and storing a centroid ID per piece. This course goes to the extreme: **one bit per dimension**. The motivation is memory. One million 1024-dimensional float32 embeddings take 1,000,000 x 1024 x 4 bytes = **4.1 GB**. Stored as one bit per dimension they take **128 MB**, a 32x cut, small enough to keep in RAM and scan quickly. For comparison, **int8 scalar quantization** maps each coordinate's range onto 256 evenly spaced levels and stores the level number in one byte, a 4x cut.

blocks.title: Bytes per 1024-dimensional vector

scenes.caption: float32 stores 4 bytes per dimension: 4096 bytes per vector. int8 scalar quantization stores 1 byte per dimension: 1024 bytes, a 4x cut.
Binary quantization keeps 1 bit per dimension: 1024 bits = 128 bytes, exactly 32x smaller than float32.
RaBitQ (from lesson 3 on) also stores 1 bit per dimension plus two float32 correction factors per vector: 136 bytes, about 30x smaller.

blocks.md: The simplest scheme, **binary quantization (BQ)**, is what the `quantize_embeddings` function of sentence-transformers (Hugging Face's Python library for embedding models) does. It thresholds every coordinate at zero: the bit is 1 if the value is positive and 0 otherwise. Write $D$ for the number of dimensions: a 1024-dimensional vector ($D = 1024$) becomes a 1024-bit string, which is sixteen 64-bit words.

To compare two bit strings, count the positions where they differ. That count is the **Hamming distance**, written $H$. On a CPU it is an XOR of the two words (1 wherever bits differ) followed by **popcount**, an instruction that counts the 1 bits in a word. For 1024 bits that is 16 XORs and 16 popcounts, with no floating-point math at all.

blocks.title: From floats to bits to Hamming distance (D = 8)

scenes.caption: A toy query and document with 8 dimensions. Their cosine similarity is 0.979: they point in almost the same direction.
Threshold at zero: positive values become 1, the rest 0. Each 4-byte float is now one bit.
Dimension 2 is the only disagreement: 0.05 in the query versus -0.04 in the document. Two tiny values on opposite sides of zero flip a whole bit.
XOR marks the differing positions, and popcount of the XOR gives the Hamming distance: H = 1.

blocks.md: Angle brackets around two vectors mean their inner product (dot product): $\langle s, t\rangle$ is the sum of $s_i t_i$ over all $D$ dimensions. If you map bit 1 to +1 and bit 0 to -1, the dot product of two such sign vectors is a simple function of the Hamming distance $H$: each agreeing position adds +1 and each disagreeing position adds -1.

blocks.caption: For sign vectors s and t of length D. Ranking by smallest Hamming distance is the same as ranking by largest sign dot product (the docs of Qdrant, an open-source vector database, use the same identity).

blocks.prompt: Three more documents have true cosine similarity to the query of 0.862 (B), 0.128 (C) and 0.905 (D). Their Hamming distances to the query are B = 2, C = 2 and D = 1, with A = 1. What does a pure Hamming ranking get wrong?
blocks.reveal: It cannot separate **B from C**: both have H = 2, even though B is a near match (0.862) and C is nearly unrelated (0.128). A and D also tie at H = 1. With 8 bits there are only 9 possible distances, so ties are common. Real embeddings have far more bits, but the same coarseness shows up among close candidates, which is exactly where ranking matters.

blocks.title: Bit agreement vs true cosine for docs A to D

scenes.caption: Fraction of matching bits, (D - H) / D. A and D tie at 0.875, B and C tie at 0.75.
True cosine similarity of the float vectors: 0.979, 0.862, 0.128, 0.905. The bits lost the gap between B and C entirely.

blocks.md: Sign bits only carry information if coordinates are spread around zero. Qdrant's docs say binary quantization needs a *centered distribution* of vector components. If every coordinate is positive, every bit is 1 and all vectors look identical; non-negative data such as SIFT (scale-invariant feature transform) image descriptors comes close to this. Lesson 2 measures this failure.
Binary quantization = sign of each coordinate, compared with XOR and popcount. It buys 32x memory and very cheap comparisons, but the distance it produces is coarse and has no error guarantee.

blocks.question: Two 1024-bit codes have Hamming distance 312. What is the dot product of the corresponding +1/-1 sign vectors?
blocks.explain: Dot = D - 2H = 1024 - 624 = 400. Each of the 712 agreeing positions adds +1 and each of the 312 differing positions adds -1: 712 - 312 = 400.

blocks.question: Which data would make plain sign-bit quantization nearly useless?
options: Unit-normalized text embeddings with coordinates spread around zero
Vectors with 4096 dimensions instead of 1024
Queries that are not in the indexed set
Vectors whose coordinates are all non-negative, such as histogram features
blocks.explain: With all coordinates at or above zero, almost every bit is 1, so codes barely differ. More dimensions helps binary quantization (more bits), and unseen queries are the normal case.

lessons.title: Binary search plus rescoring: oversample, then re-rank

blocks.md: Because Hamming distance is coarse, nobody returns binary results directly. The standard pipeline has two stages. **Stage 1** scans the compact binary codes and keeps more candidates than you need. **Stage 2** recomputes the similarity of just those candidates with more precise vectors and returns the best $k$, the number of results the caller asked for. The extra fetch is set by **oversampling** (Qdrant, a factor), the **rescore multiplier** (sentence-transformers, a factor) or **rescoreLimit** (Weaviate, another open-source vector database; an absolute number of objects).

blocks.title: Binary candidate search with rescoring

scenes.caption: The float query is thresholded into bits, just like the stored vectors.
Stage 1 scans every binary code (or walks an index over them) using XOR and popcount. This is the cheap part.
Keep k x oversampling candidates. In Qdrant's example, limit 100 with oversampling 2.4 pre-selects 240 vectors.
Stage 2 fetches only those candidates' original vectors and scores them against the float query. If originals live on disk, this step costs one random read per candidate.
Return the best k by exact similarity. Recall now depends on whether the true neighbors made it into the candidate set.

blocks.md: How much does stage 2 recover? The sentence-transformers team measured Mixedbread's `mxbai-embed-large-v1` embedding model on the retrieval tasks of MTEB (the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark). Quality there is **NDCG@10**: each relevant result in the top 10 earns credit divided by log base 2 of (rank + 1), so higher ranks count more, and the total is divided by the score of a perfect ordering, so 1.0 is perfect. The name lists those steps: a gain per relevant result, discounted by rank, accumulated, then normalized. On that measure binary embeddings kept **92.53%** of float32 retrieval quality, and rescoring the top results with the float32 query against the binary document vectors raised that to **96.45%**, with memory cut 32x. Recall@k, from the vector search course, is the fraction of the true $k$ nearest neighbors that appear among the $k$ results. Qdrant reports 0.98 recall@100 with 4x oversampling for 1536-dimensional vectors from OpenAI's `text-embedding-ada-002` embedding model.

To see the knob directly, I ran a small simulation (numpy, fixed seed): 20,000 synthetic vectors with D = 1024, each a random mix of 64 shared hidden directions (latent factors) plus independent noise, and 200 queries. Ground truth is the exact top 10 by cosine. Stage 1 ranks by Hamming distance, stage 2 rescores with exact cosine on the original vectors.

blocks.prompt: With oversampling 1 (fetch exactly 10 candidates, then rescore them), does recall@10 improve over returning the Hamming top 10 directly?
blocks.reveal: **No.** Recall@10 only asks which 10 items you returned, and rescoring 10 candidates just reorders the same 10. In the simulation both give **0.562**. Rescoring can only improve the *set* when you fetch more than k. (Hugging Face saw a gain at multiplier 1 because they rescored a top 100 and scored NDCG@10, which rewards better order and lets rescoring change which items reach the top 10.)

blocks.title: Simulated recall@10 vs oversampling (D = 1024)

scenes.caption: Centered data (half the bits are 1): recall climbs from 0.562 to 0.759, 0.917 and 0.982 as stage 1 hands more candidates to stage 2. Simplified synthetic data, not a real embedding model.
Same data shifted so most coordinates are positive (88.5% of bits are 1). Hamming distance is nearly uninformative: 0.179, 0.274, 0.384, 0.52. Oversampling cannot rescue a broken first stage cheaply.

blocks.md: Two details matter in practice. First, **what you rescore with**. Qdrant and Weaviate rescore with the original float vectors, which must be stored somewhere: Qdrant warns that rescoring can significantly slow search when originals are on disk. The Hugging Face demo over 41 million Wikipedia texts keeps a 5.2 GB binary index in memory and loads int8 vectors for the top 40 from a 47.5 GB on-disk index. Second, the query does not have to be binary: scoring a float or int8 query against binary documents (**asymmetric** scoring) keeps more information at no storage cost.
Oversampling is a query-time knob: it trades speed for recall without rebuilding the index. Tune it on held-out queries for your own data, since the right value varies by model and dimension.

blocks.question: Your binary index is in RAM and original vectors are on an SSD. Recall is too low at oversampling 2. What is the main cost of raising oversampling to 8?
options: The binary index gets 4x larger
Queries must be re-embedded
Stage 2 reads about 4x more original vectors from disk per query
The Hamming scan must use floating-point math
blocks.explain: The binary scan cost barely changes. Stage 2 work, mostly random SSD reads of original vectors, grows with the number of candidates, so going from 2k to 8k candidates is about 4x more reads.

blocks.question: Why does binary quantization pair so naturally with rescoring, compared with int8 scalar quantization?
options: Binary distances are coarse with many ties, so a cheap wide first pass plus a precise second pass recovers most quality
Binary codes cannot be stored in RAM without rescoring
Rescoring is impossible with int8 vectors
Binary distances are biased upward, and rescoring subtracts the bias
blocks.explain: 1 bit per dimension loses a lot of ranking detail, so the first stage is best used as a filter. Rescoring works with int8 too (Hugging Face shows it), it just matters less there.

lessons.title: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs

blocks.md: RaBitQ (Jianyang Gao and Cheng Long, SIGMOD 2024, the ACM conference on management of data) also stores a $D$-bit string per vector, but it designs the codebook so that the distance estimate is **unbiased** (averaged over its random choices, it equals the true value) and has a **proven error bound**. The paper's motivation is that PQ and its variants have no error bound and can fail badly: on the MSong dataset (992,272 audio feature vectors with 420 dimensions), PQ's fast-scan variant had over 50% average relative error in estimated distances and could not reach 60% recall even with re-ranking.

**Step 1: normalize.** Let $o_r$ be a raw data vector, $q_r$ the raw query, and $c$ a centroid (in practice the IVF cluster centroid the vector belongs to; until lesson 6 the course uses one global centroid). RaBitQ subtracts the centroid and divides by the length of what is left, the norm $\|o_r - c\|$, giving the unit vector $o = (o_r - c)/\|o_r - c\|$: the offset from the centroid divided by its own length. Likewise the query becomes the unit vector $q = (q_r - c)/\|q_r - c\|$. With many IVF clusters each vector is normalized against its own centroid, so the query is re-centered once per probed cluster (lesson 6). The squared distance between raw vectors then depends only on two stored norms and one inner product of unit vectors:

blocks.caption: Equation (2) of the paper, in words: the squared raw distance is the data vector's squared distance to c, plus the query's, minus 2 times both distances times the unit inner product of q and o. The first is stored per vector; the query's is computed once per query.

blocks.md: Where it comes from: the difference of the raw vectors is the data vector's offset from the centroid minus the query's offset, $o_r - q_r = (o_r - c) - (q_r - c)$. The squared length of a difference is the two squared lengths minus twice their inner product, and the inner product of two vectors is their two lengths times the inner product of their unit directions, which is $\langle q, o\rangle$. So everything reduces to estimating that one unit inner product.

**Step 2: the codebook.** The candidate quantized vectors are the corners of a hypercube, 2 to the power $D$ of them, scaled onto the unit sphere: every coordinate is $+1/\sqrt{D}$ or $-1/\sqrt{D}$. Centering by $c$ is what fixes the all-positive failure from lesson 1, since coordinates of $o_r - c$ are spread around zero.

blocks.prompt: Without any rotation, how well does this hypercube codebook fit the vector (1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0) in D = 8? Its best corner is (1, 1, ..., 1) scaled by 1/sqrt(8). Guess the inner product between the vector and its quantized vector.
blocks.reveal: Only $1/\sqrt{8} = 0.354$, a squared distance of $2 - 2/\sqrt{8} = 1.293$. A vector like (1, 1, ..., 1)/sqrt(8) would be quantized perfectly (inner product 1). A fixed codebook favors some directions and is terrible for others, so any error bound would depend on the data.

blocks.md: **Step 3: rotate.** RaBitQ samples a random orthogonal matrix $P$: a matrix whose transpose is its inverse, so it preserves lengths and angles, which is a rotation (possibly with a reflection). It uses the rotated corners $P x$ as the codebook. A uniformly random rotation can send any corner anywhere on the sphere, so no direction is favored. Only $P$ is stored; the 2 to the power $D$ codewords are never materialized. Applying a dense $P$ is not free: it costs $D^2$ multiply-adds per vector and per query (about a million at $D = 1024$), which is why libraries use the structured rotations of lesson 6. The paper calls this a type of Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, the family of random linear maps named after a 1984 lemma by Johnson and Lindenstrauss, which shows that a random projection keeps distances between points within a small error. A rotation keeps lengths exactly; what RaBitQ uses is its randomness.

Finding the nearest rotated corner is cheap. Rotations preserve inner products, so the inner product of $o$ with a rotated corner, $\langle o, P x\rangle$, equals $\langle P^{-1} o, x\rangle$: apply the inverse rotation to the data vector once and compare it with the plain corners. Write $o' = P^{-1} o$. The inner product, which is $\sum_i x_i o'_i$ with $x_i = \pm 1/\sqrt{D}$, is largest when every term is positive, so the best corner just copies the **signs** of $o'$. The stored code is those $D$ sign bits.

blocks.title: Encoding one unit vector with RaBitQ (D = 8)

scenes.caption: A spiky unit vector: most of its length sits in dimension 0. Signs taken directly would match it with inner product only 0.673.
Apply the inverse of a random rotation (seed 11). The length is now spread across all 8 coordinates; the vector still has norm 1.
The code is the sign pattern of o': 11100110. That is the whole per-dimension payload, 1 bit each.
The bits stand for the corner x-bar with entries plus or minus 1/sqrt(8) = 0.354. Its inner product with o' is sum of |o'_i| / sqrt(8) = 0.873, far better than 0.673 without rotation.

blocks.caption: Here o-bar = P x-bar is the quantized vector. Rotating both by P inverse leaves the inner product unchanged, and x-bar has the sign of each o'_i, so each coordinate adds |o'_i| / sqrt(D). This value is computed once at index time and stored next to the code.

blocks.md: Why it is about 0.8: after a random rotation, each coordinate of $o'$ behaves like a normal variable with standard deviation $1/\sqrt{D}$, and the average absolute value of a normal is its standard deviation times $\sqrt{2/\pi}$. Adding $D$ such values and dividing by $\sqrt{D}$ gives $\sqrt{2/\pi} = 0.798$. The paper's exact formula gives 0.798 to 0.800 for $D$ from 100 to 1,000,000, and it is 0.823 at $D = 8$.

Per vector, RaBitQ therefore stores the $D$-bit code plus two floats: the norm $\|o_r - c\|$ (the data vector's distance to the centroid) and $\langle \bar o, o\rangle$. The paper pads the code length to the next multiple of 64 so codes fit 64-bit words. Index time is similar to PQ: on GIST (one million 960-dimensional vectors, 32 threads) the paper reports 117 s for RaBitQ, 105 s for PQ and 291 s for OPQ (optimized product quantization, which learns a rotation before PQ).

The rotation does not make every vector quantize well on every draw. It makes the quality *random with a known distribution*, the same for every input direction. That is what turns "works on my dataset" into a guarantee that holds regardless of the data.
RaBitQ indexing: center and normalize, apply one random rotation, store the sign bits plus two floats per vector. The codebook is the rotated hypercube, so no k-means training is needed.

blocks.question: Why does RaBitQ apply P^-1 to each data vector instead of rotating the codebook?
options: Rotating 2^D codewords is impossible to store or search; rotating one vector and reading its signs finds the same nearest codeword
P^-1 is cheaper to compute than P
The codebook must stay axis-aligned for popcount to work
It makes the code shorter than D bits
blocks.explain: Inner products are invariant under rotation, so maximizing over P x is the same as maximizing over x against P^-1 o, which is solved by copying signs. The codebook stays conceptual.

blocks.question: After rotation, the inner product between a data vector and its quantized vector is about 0.8 in high dimensions. What does this number mean?
options: The code is wrong in 20% of the bits
The estimator is accurate to within 0.2
The quantized vector is a unit vector at roughly 37 degrees from the data vector, so using it directly would shrink inner products
Only 80% of vectors get a valid code
blocks.explain: Both are unit vectors and their cosine is about 0.8 (about 37 degrees). Lesson 4 shows why treating o-bar as if it were o is biased, and how dividing by this stored 0.8-ish value fixes it.

lessons.title: The unbiased estimator and its O(1/sqrt(D)) error

blocks.md: At query time we want $\langle o, q\rangle$ but only have the code. The obvious move, and what PQ does, is to pretend the quantized vector is the data vector and use $\langle \bar o, q\rangle$. RaBitQ instead looks at the geometry. Split $q$ into its part along $o$ and the rest. Since $q$ is a unit vector, its part along $o$ has length $\langle o, q\rangle$, and by Pythagoras the rest has length $\sqrt{1 - \langle o, q\rangle^2}$; call its unit direction $e_1$, which is orthogonal to $o$. So $q = \langle o, q\rangle\, o + \sqrt{1 - \langle o, q\rangle^2}\, e_1$. Taking the inner product of both sides with $\bar o$ gives the paper's Lemma 3.1:

blocks.tex: \langle \bar o, q\rangle = \langle \bar o, o\rangle\,\langle o, q\rangle + \langle \bar o, e_1\rangle\,\sqrt{1 - \langle o, q\rangle^2}
blocks.caption: Exact for any three unit vectors. The first term is the signal, scaled by about 0.8. The second term is noise: its factor is the projection of the random o-bar onto a direction orthogonal to o.

blocks.md: Dividing by the stored $\langle \bar o, o\rangle$ removes the scaling. Because the rotation is uniformly random, $\langle \bar o, e_1\rangle$ is symmetric around 0, so the leftover error term has expectation exactly 0. That gives the RaBitQ estimator, and through equation (2) also an unbiased estimate of squared Euclidean distance:

blocks.tex: \widehat{\langle o, q\rangle} = \frac{\langle \bar o, q\rangle}{\langle \bar o, o\rangle} = \langle o, q\rangle + \sqrt{1 - \langle o, q\rangle^2}\;\frac{\langle \bar o, e_1\rangle}{\langle \bar o, o\rangle}
blocks.caption: The estimator divides the code's inner product with the query by the stored factor. It equals the truth plus a noise term: the projection of o-bar onto e_1, divided by the stored factor, times sqrt(1 - <o,q>^2). Theorem 3.2: its expected value is the true inner product.

blocks.md: Back to the toy from lesson 3 (seed 11). The query, after the same inverse rotation and normalization, has true inner product $\langle o, q\rangle = 0.688$ with the data vector. The code gives $\langle \bar o, q\rangle = 0.530$ and the stored factor is $\langle \bar o, o\rangle = 0.873$, so the estimate is $0.530 / 0.873 = 0.607$, an error of -0.080. A different rotation (seed 32) gives $0.395 / 0.886 = 0.446$, error -0.242. At D = 8 single estimates are noisy. The claim is about the average and about how the noise shrinks with D.

blocks.title: Toy pair, D = 8, averaged over 20,000 random rotations

scenes.caption: The target: the true inner product of the toy pair is 0.688.
Treating the quantized vector as the data vector averages 0.567: biased low by the factor E<o-bar,o>, which is 0.823 at D = 8.
Dividing by the stored <o-bar,o> averages 0.688, matching the truth. Individual draws still scatter (standard deviation 0.195 at D = 8).

blocks.md: How big is the noise? Fix the stored factor $\langle \bar o, o\rangle$. The rest of $\bar o$ has length $\sqrt{1 - \langle \bar o, o\rangle^2}$ and, because the rotation is uniformly random, points in a uniformly random direction among the $D - 1$ directions orthogonal to $o$. A random unit vector in $D - 1$ dimensions has a projection onto a fixed direction such as $e_1$ of typical size $1/\sqrt{D-1}$. So $\langle \bar o, e_1\rangle$ concentrates within order $1/\sqrt{D}$ of 0. The paper turns this into a bound with a confidence knob $\epsilon_0$ (larger means wider and safer): with probability at least $1 - 2e^{-c_0 \epsilon_0^2}$, where $c_0$ is a fixed constant from the concentration inequality, the error obeys:

blocks.tex: \left|\frac{\langle \bar o, q\rangle}{\langle \bar o, o\rangle} - \langle o, q\rangle\right| \le \sqrt{\frac{1 - \langle \bar o, o\rangle^2}{\langle \bar o, o\rangle^2}}\cdot\frac{\epsilon_0}{\sqrt{D-1}} = O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\right)
blocks.caption: In words: the error is at most epsilon_0 / sqrt(D - 1), times the square root of 1 minus the stored factor squared, over the stored factor (about 0.75 at 0.8). The paper fixes epsilon_0 = 1.9. Alon and Klartag (FOCS 2017) showed no D-bit code beats O(1/sqrt(D)): the bound is asymptotically optimal.

blocks.title: Estimator error shrinks like 1/sqrt(D)

scenes.caption: Dots: measured standard deviation of the error over 4,000 random rotations per D, true inner product (ip) 0.688. The curve sqrt(1 - ip^2) x 0.755 / sqrt(D - 1) is a first-order approximation using E<o-bar,o> = 0.798.
Each 4x increase in D halves the error: 0.140 at D = 16, 0.0689 at 64, 0.0338 at 256, 0.0171 at 1024. Higher-dimensional embeddings are easier for 1-bit codes.
Pairs that are nearly orthogonal (ip near 0) have the largest error; near-duplicates (ip near 1) have almost none, because the noise term is scaled by sqrt(1 - ip^2).
The bound with eps0 = 1.9 and <o-bar,o> = 0.8 sits at about 1.9 standard deviations, 1.9x the typical error at ip = 0, and it is what RaBitQ uses to decide re-ranking (lesson 5).

blocks.md: Those are the paper's equations (14) to (16). It picked $\epsilon_0 = 1.9$ because, in its experiments, deciding re-ranking with this bound gave nearly perfect recall of the true nearest neighbor. That is not the same as covering every pair: in my simulation the 1.9 interval missed the true value for about 1% of pairs at $\langle o, q\rangle = 0.69$ and about 6% at $\langle o, q\rangle = 0$. Near neighbors are the pairs that matter for search, and their larger inner products give smaller errors.

Unbiased does not mean accurate on each pair. It means the errors average out to zero instead of pushing every estimate the same way. Per-pair accuracy comes from concentration: the 1/sqrt(D) shrinkage.

blocks.question: RaBitQ errors at D = 256 are too large for you. Following the 1/sqrt(D) rule, how many code bits per vector would halve the error?
blocks.explain: Error scales as 1/sqrt(D), so halving it needs 4x the bits: 1024. The paper notes you can lengthen codes by padding vectors with zeros before rotation; padded dimensions are not kept in the raw vectors.

blocks.question: A colleague estimates inner products with <o-bar,q> directly, skipping the division. What happens to a ranking of documents for one query?
options: Nothing; the ranking is identical because every estimate is scaled by exactly the same constant
Estimates become unbiased but noisier
Each document's estimate is scaled by its own <o-bar,o>, which varies per vector, so the ranking gets extra noise and the distances are biased
The code must be recomputed
blocks.explain: The scaling factor is not a global constant: it is about 0.8 on average but differs from vector to vector, because it depends on how evenly each rotated vector spreads its length. The paper also notes this direct estimator is provably biased, which matters when plugged into equation (2) for distances.

lessons.title: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound

blocks.md: The estimator needs $\langle \bar o, q\rangle = \langle \bar x, q'\rangle$ where $q' = P^{-1} q$ is computed once per query. Since the estimate is approximate anyway, RaBitQ also quantizes $q'$: with $v_l = \min_i q'_i$, $v_r = \max_i q'_i$ and step $\Delta = (v_r - v_l)/(2^{B_q} - 1)$, each coordinate becomes a $B_q$-bit integer $\bar q_u[i]$: subtract $v_l$, divide by $\Delta$ and round, giving a whole number from 0 to 15 when $B_q = 4$. The paper uses **randomized rounding** (round up with probability equal to the fractional part) so the query quantization stays unbiased, and proves $B_q = \Theta(\log\log D)$ bits suffice. In practice $B_q = 4$; Faiss (Meta's open-source library for vector similarity search) uses `qb = 4` by default.

For the toy query, $v_l = -0.403$, $v_r = 0.514$, $\Delta = 0.0612$, and rounding gives $\bar q_u$ = (6, 6, 15, 8, 10, 15, 15, 0). (For a readable toy I rounded to nearest; RaBitQ rounds randomly.) Each query value is now approximated as $v_l + \Delta\,\bar q_u[i]$, a fixed offset plus a step times an integer (an *affine* quantization). Expanding the inner product of a sign vector with this affine-quantized vector gives terms that are all precomputed except one integer dot product:

blocks.tex: \langle \bar x, \bar q\rangle = \frac{2\Delta}{\sqrt D}\langle \bar x_b, \bar q_u\rangle + \frac{2 v_l}{\sqrt D}\sum_i \bar x_b[i] - \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt D}\sum_i \bar q_u[i] - \sqrt D\, v_l
blocks.caption: Equation (20), in words: 2 Delta over sqrt(D) times the bits-by-integers dot product, plus 2 v_l over sqrt(D) times the code's popcount (stored at index time), minus Delta over sqrt(D) times the query integers' sum, minus sqrt(D) times v_l.

blocks.md: Where it comes from: the stored bits $\bar x_b$ stand for the corner $\bar x$. Bit 1 means $+1/\sqrt{D}$ and bit 0 means $-1/\sqrt{D}$, so a coordinate with bit $b$ is $(2b - 1)/\sqrt{D}$. Multiply each coordinate by $v_l + \Delta\,\bar q_u[i]$ and sum. Bits times integers give the first term, bits times $v_l$ give the popcount term, and the minus ones give the last two. Everything except the first term is per query or stored, so only the dot product of bits with small integers is computed per vector.

Split each 4-bit query integer into 4 bit planes. Then $\langle \bar x_b, \bar q_u\rangle = \sum_j 2^j\,\mathrm{popcount}(\bar x_b \,\&\, \text{plane}_j)$: four AND plus popcount passes over $D$-bit strings, the same instructions plain binary quantization uses.

blocks.title: Bit-plane dot product for the toy (D = 8, Bq = 4)
blocks.code:
xb = [1,1,1,0,0,1,1,0]          # data code: signs of o'
qu = [6,6,15,8,10,15,15,0]       # query, 4-bit integers
acc = 0
for j in range(4):               # one pass per bit plane
    plane = [(v >> j) & 1 for v in qu]
    both = [a & b for a, b in zip(xb, plane)]
    acc += (1 << j) * sum(both)  # sum(both) = popcount
# acc == dot(xb, qu) == 57

scenes.caption: The data code from lesson 3 and the 4-bit query. In real code each list is packed into 64-bit words.

blocks.md: Plugging in (code popcount 5, query sum 75) gives $\langle \bar x, \bar q\rangle = 0.558$ versus 0.530 with the float query, so the estimate is $0.558/0.873 = 0.640$ instead of 0.607. At D = 8 with nearest rounding, query quantization error is visible; averaged over 20,000 randomized roundings the value is 0.530, unbiased. For a single code, the paper reports this bitwise path is on average about 3x faster than PQ and OPQ looking up tables in RAM at the same accuracy. For packed batches of 32 codes, RaBitQ reuses PQ's SIMD **FastScan** layout by treating each 4 bits of the code as a sub-segment with a 16-entry lookup table.

**FastScan, by hand.** The single-code path above does $B_q$ AND plus popcount passes per code. The batch path turns the same dot product into table lookups, exactly the shape of PQ fast scan (see the *Product quantization* course, lesson *PQ fast scan: 4-bit codes, SIMD lookups and 8-bit tables*). Split the 8-bit toy code 11100110 into two 4-bit segments, 1110 (dimensions 0 to 3) and 0110 (dimensions 4 to 7). For each segment, precompute once per query a 16-entry table: entry $p$ is the sum of the query integers $\bar q_u[i]$ over the positions where the 4-bit pattern $p$ has a 1. Read a pattern left to right in dimension order, so 1110 is entry 14.

blocks.title: Two 16-entry lookup tables replace the bit-plane passes (toy)

scenes.caption: Segment 1 covers query integers 6, 6, 15, 8. Entry p adds the values whose bit is set: entry 1 (0001) is 8, entry 2 (0010) is 15, entry 15 (1111) is 6+6+15+8 = 35.
Segment 2 covers 10, 15, 15, 0. Entry 6 (0110) is 15+15 = 30. The tables depend only on the query, so they are built once and reused for every code in the list.
The code's first segment 1110 is entry 14 of table 1: 6+6+15 = 27.
Its second segment 0110 is entry 6 of table 2: 30. Two lookups and one add give 27 + 30 = 57, the same value as the four bit-plane passes.

blocks.md: A $D$-bit code needs $D/4$ lookups. FastScan makes them fast in batches: the paper packs 32 codes together, keeps tables of 8-bit entries in SIMD registers (one 16-entry table takes 128 bits, so an AVX2 register holds two; RaBitQ's entries are sums of at most four 4-bit values, at most 60, so they fit exactly) and uses a shuffle instruction to look up one segment of all 32 codes at once. The paper notes that RaBitQ and PQ both reach higher throughput this way than one code at a time, but only when codes can be packed into batches. An IVF list is a natural batch; the next lesson shows why graph indexes are not.

**Re-ranking by the bound.** PQ systems re-rank a fixed number of candidates, a knob that must be tuned per dataset. RaBitQ turns its error bound into a lower bound on each candidate's distance: through equation (2), an inner-product error of at most $e$ is a distance error of at most 2 times the two centroid distances times $e$, so the estimated distance minus that amount is a lower bound. Scanning candidates, it computes the exact distance only if that lower bound is below the best exact distance found so far; otherwise the candidate is provably (with high probability) not the nearest neighbor and is dropped.

No exact distance is known yet, so the first candidate is re-ranked: exact 1.100. Best so far = 1.100.
Candidates 2 to 5 have lower bounds 1.019 to 1.099, all below 1.100, so each might still be closer. Re-rank them: none beats 1.100.
Candidates 6 to 8 have lower bounds 1.109, 1.132 and 1.141, above the best exact 1.100. They are dropped without touching their raw vectors.

Over all 20,000 vectors, only 5 exact distances were computed and the true nearest neighbor (exact 1.100) was found. Simplified: the paper does this inside probed IVF clusters with per-cluster centroids (next lesson).

blocks.md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

blocks.question: Why can the error bound replace the usual 'rerank the top R candidates' hyperparameter?
options: The bound gives each candidate a lower bound on its distance, so you can skip exactly those that cannot beat the best exact distance found so far
The bound makes every estimate exact
The bound tells you the optimal R for each dataset ahead of time
Re-ranking is not needed for RaBitQ at all
blocks.explain: A fixed R must be tuned and can be too small on hard data (the paper shows no single R works across datasets). The bound adapts per query: easy queries re-rank few vectors, hard ones more.

blocks.question: RaBitQ quantizes the query to 4-bit integers. What does it gain, and why is it safe?
options: It shrinks the index 4x; safe because queries are not stored
It makes the estimator exact; safe because rounding is random
It removes the need for the rotation
It turns the per-vector float dot product into a few AND plus popcount passes; safe because the added error is much smaller than the estimator's own O(1/sqrt(D)) error
blocks.explain: The code is already a 1-bit approximation, so computing its inner product in full float precision is overkill. Theorem 3.3 shows Theta(log log D) query bits keep the added error at the same order, and 4 bits made it negligible in the paper's tests.

lessons.title: RaBitQ inside an index: IVF clusters, graphs and fast rotations

blocks.md: Every example so far used one global centroid $c$. Real deployments put RaBitQ inside an index. With IVF (the inverted file index: k-means splits the data into clusters and a query scans only the `nprobe` clusters whose centroids are nearest, as in the *Vector search and ANN* course), the RaBitQ paper normalizes each vector against **its own cluster's centroid** $c_k$. The offsets from a nearby centroid are smaller and spread around zero, which is what sign bits need. The price is that the query must be centered on each probed cluster's centroid in turn.

blocks.caption: The rotated, normalized query for probed cluster k. Because P inverse is linear, P^-1 q_r is computed once per query and each P^-1 c_k once at index time, so re-centering costs one vector subtraction and one scaling per probed cluster.

blocks.md: The divisor $\|q_r - c_k\|$ is free too: IVF already computed the squared distance from the query to every centroid to choose which clusters to probe. Then, per probed cluster, RaBitQ quantizes $q'_k$ to $B_q = 4$ bits with its own $v_l$, $v_r$ and $\Delta$ (lesson 5), since $q'_k$ differs from cluster to cluster. That is $O(D)$ work per probed cluster. Per vector in the list the cost is unchanged: a few AND plus popcount passes (or FastScan lookups) and a handful of multiply-adds with the stored factors.

Per vector in the list: estimate the distance and its lower bound from the code and two stored floats.
Only vectors whose lower bound beats the best exact distance so far get an exact distance. The rest are dropped.

Stored factors $\langle \bar o, o\rangle$ range from 0.71 to 0.875 (mean 0.80), so at $D = 64$ the bound with $\epsilon_0 = 1.9$ is about 0.18 in inner product: wide.

blocks.md: **The rotation's own cost.** A dense random orthogonal $P$ costs $D^2$ multiply-adds per vector at index time and per query, and $D^2$ floats of storage: at $D = 1024$ about 1.05 million multiply-adds and 4.2 MB; at $D = 1536$, 2.36 million and 9.4 MB. RaBitQ-Library's default **FHT/Kac rotator** replaces it with a structured transform. The **Hadamard transform** of size $2^m$ mixes pairs of coordinates $(a, b)$ into $((a+b)/\sqrt2, (a-b)/\sqrt2)$ in $m$ passes, so it costs about $D \log_2 D$ additions instead of $D^2$. The library runs 4 rounds of random sign flips plus a normalized fast Hadamard transform, and when $D$ is not a power of two it adds a Givens step: each coordinate of the first half is paired with its partner in the second half and the pair is rotated by a fixed angle $\pi/4$, which mixes the halves. It pads $D$ to a multiple of 32, stores just $4D$ random sign bits, and approximates the uniform random rotation the analysis assumes.

blocks.title: Rotation work per vector (approximate operation counts)

scenes.caption: Dense matrix: D^2 multiply-adds, 16,384 at D = 128, 589,824 at 768 and 2,359,296 at 1536. Quadratic growth dominates for modern embedding sizes.
FHT/Kac, simplified count (4 rounds of butterflies on the largest power-of-two block, sign flips and a Givens step): about 4,096, 24,576 and 53,248. That is 4x, 24x and 44x less work.

blocks.md: Two details from the library docs: the padded dimension is part of the rotation, so changing the padding changes the sampled rotation and the codes even with the same seed; and data, centroids and queries must all use the same rotator. SymphonyQG (Section 3.1.4) describes the same move as a fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform based on the Hadamard transform, cutting rotation from $O(D^2)$ to $O(D \log D)$. Weaviate's rotational quantization also uses a fast rotation based on the Walsh-Hadamard transform, which its docs say takes about 7 to 10 microseconds for a 1536-dimensional vector.

**Graphs are different.** HNSW-style search visits one vertex at a time and decides where to go next, so the vectors to score are not known in advance and cannot be packed into FastScan batches; the RaBitQ paper lists this as the reason it evaluated IVF. NGT-QG (in Yahoo Japan's NGT library) solved the layout problem by storing, next to each vertex, a copy of the quantized codes of all its neighbors, so one sequential read and one FastScan batch estimate the whole neighbor list. SymphonyQG (Gou, Gao, Xu and Long, 2024) does this with RaBitQ. A graph has no cluster centroids, so it centers each neighbor's code on the **vertex itself**; a vector that neighbors two vertices therefore has two different codes. It also makes every vertex's neighbor count a multiple of the batch size and avoids NGT-QG's separate re-ranking step.

blocks.md: In practice: RaBitQ-Library ships three indexes, IVF-RaBitQ (partitioned search with batch scoring), HNSW-RaBitQ (graph traversal over quantized vectors) and SymphonyQG (graph search with batched estimation; updates require a rebuild). Faiss has `IndexIVFRaBitQ` and also an HNSW variant (`HNSW32,RaBitQ` in its index factory). The SymphonyQG paper reports 1.5x to 4.5x the queries per second of the most competitive baselines at 95% recall on its datasets.

Per-cluster centering means a code only makes sense together with its centroid. Moving a vector to another IVF list, or changing a centroid, requires re-encoding it; in SymphonyQG a vector is encoded once per vertex that links to it, so memory grows with the number of edges.

Inside an index, RaBitQ adds O(D) work per probed cluster (re-center and quantize the query) and nothing per vector. Rotate the query once, precompute rotated centroids, and use a structured O(D log D) rotation instead of a dense D x D matrix.

blocks.question: A team rotates every query with a dense 1536 x 1536 matrix and serves 100,000 queries per second. What does the rotation alone cost, and what is the fix?
options: About 2.4 million multiply-adds per probed cluster per query; probe fewer clusters
Nothing measurable, since the rotation is applied only at index time
About 2.4 million multiply-adds per query, roughly 2.4 x 10^11 per second; switch to a Hadamard-based rotation such as FHT/Kac, about 53 thousand operations per query
About 1,536 multiply-adds per query; no fix needed
blocks.explain: 1536^2 = 2,359,296 multiply-adds per query, once per query (re-centering per cluster is only a subtraction). At 100k QPS that is about 2.4 x 10^11 per second just to rotate. A structured transform cuts it to O(D log D), about 44x less here, and stores 4D sign bits instead of a 9.4 MB matrix.

blocks.question: With nprobe = 8, why does IVF-RaBitQ not multiply the query by P^-1 eight times?
options: Each cluster uses its own random rotation
P^-1 is linear: P^-1 (q_r - c_k) = P^-1 q_r - P^-1 c_k, and P^-1 c_k is stored at index time
The query is not normalized in IVF-RaBitQ
Only the first probed cluster needs a rotated query
blocks.explain: One rotation of the raw query plus one stored rotated centroid per cluster gives every re-centered query by subtraction; dividing by the already known centroid distance normalizes it. All clusters share one rotation P.

blocks.question: Why do quantized graph indexes such as NGT-QG and SymphonyQG copy neighbors' codes into each vertex's record instead of storing each code once?
options: Graph search scores a vertex's neighbors together, so co-locating their codes turns random reads into one sequential read and one FastScan batch
Each copy uses fewer bits than a shared code
It removes the need for a rotation
FastScan requires every code to appear exactly 32 times
blocks.explain: The bottleneck of graph search is random memory access per neighbor. Duplicating codes costs memory but makes each step one contiguous batch. In SymphonyQG the copies also differ, because each is centered on its own vertex.

lessons.title: Extended RaBitQ: finding the best multi-bit code

blocks.md: **Extended RaBitQ** (Gao, Gou, Xu, Yang, Long and Wong, arXiv 2409.09913) answers the obvious next question: what if 32x is too aggressive and you want high recall *without* keeping raw vectors for re-ranking? It uses $B$ bits per dimension. The codebook is a uniform grid of $B$-bit unsigned integers, shifted to be symmetric around 0, normalized onto the unit sphere and randomly rotated. Because codewords are still randomly rotated unit vectors, the same estimator and its unbiasedness carry over.

**The codebook, concretely.** Take every vector whose coordinates are $B$-bit unsigned integers $u = 0, 1, \dots, 2^B - 1$ and shift them by $(2^B - 1)/2$ so the grid is symmetric around 0. For $B = 2$ each coordinate is one of -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5. Normalize each grid vector to unit length and rotate by $P$. With $B = 1$ the grid is the hypercube of lesson 3, so this is a strict generalization.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{G} = \left\{ y : y_i = -\tfrac{2^B - 1}{2} + u_i,\; u_i \in \{0, \dots, 2^B - 1\} \right\}, \qquad \mathcal{G}_r = \left\{ P\,\frac{y}{\|y\|} : y \in \mathcal{G} \right\}
blocks.caption: Equations (7) and (8) of the extended RaBitQ paper. The stored code is the integer vector u; the codebook of 2^(BD) unit vectors is never materialized, only P is stored.

blocks.title: The B = 2 grid in D = 2 and its directions

scenes.caption: All 16 grid points for D = 2, B = 2, and the angle of each after normalizing to unit length.
(0.5, 0.5) and (1.5, 1.5) point the same way, 45 degrees: after normalization they are one codeword. Only 12 of the 16 points give distinct directions.

In the first quadrant the directions are 18.4, 45 and 71.6 degrees: gaps of 26.6, but 36.8 across an axis (71.6 to 108.4). The codebook is not uniform on the circle; the random rotation is what makes its quality the same for every input direction.

blocks.md: **Why encoding is a search.** The best code is the grid vector $y$ whose direction is closest to $o' = P^{-1} o$: maximize $\langle y/\|y\|, o'\rangle$. There are $2^{BD}$ candidates, so trying them all is hopeless, and rounding $o'$ itself does not work because the grid has a fixed scale while $o'$ is a unit vector. Lemma 3.1 of the paper says the winner is the plain rounding of some rescaled vector $t \cdot o'$ for a factor $t > 0$. As $t$ grows from 0, the rounded vector changes only when some $t |o'_i|$ crosses a rounding boundary, an integer $k$. Between those **critical values** the code, and so the cosine, is constant, so only finitely many values of $t$ need checking.

blocks.caption: Work with magnitudes: the best code lies in the same orthant as o' (signs copied), so each |y_i| is a half-integer from 0.5 to 2^(B-1) - 0.5. Crossing t_(i,k) raises |y_i| from k - 0.5 to k + 0.5, which updates the dot product by |o'_i| and the squared norm by 2k in O(1).

blocks.title: Enumerating critical values for the toy vector (B = 3)

scenes.caption: t = 0: every magnitude rounds to 0.5, so the code (stored as u = y + 3.5) just copies the signs: 4 for positive, 3 for negative. Cosine 0.873, the 1-bit code of lesson 3.
First critical value t = 1/0.538 = 1.857: dimension 2 crosses 1 and moves to 1.5 (code 5). Cosine 0.886.
By t = 2.571 dimensions 7, 6 and 1 have also stepped up. Cosine 0.986: the largest coordinates now get more weight.
t = 6.438: code 5,6,7,3,3,4,7,0 with cosine 0.995, the maximum over all 24 critical values. This is the stored code.
Past the best, coordinates hit the top level 7 and stop growing while small ones keep rising: 0.990 at t = 7.713.
At t = 30.46 every coordinate is saturated at 0 or 7: the same direction as the sign code, cosine 0.873 again. The search keeps the best value seen along the way.

blocks.md: For $D = 8$ and $B = 3$ there are $8 \times 3 = 24$ critical values. In general there are about $D \cdot 2^{B-1}$; visiting them in sorted order with a min-heap is what gives the paper's $O(2^B \cdot D \log D)$ encoding time. The paper reports that a million 3,072-dimensional vectors quantize in a few minutes at the bit widths it recommends. The code below sorts all critical values at once instead of using a heap, which is simpler in numpy.

blocks.code:
def ext_encode(op, B):
    """Best B-bit extended RaBitQ code for a rotated unit vector op."""
    a = np.abs(op); D = len(a); K = 2 ** (B - 1)
    k = np.arange(1, K)
    t = (k[None, :] / a[:, None]).ravel()           # critical values k / |o'_i|
    dim = np.repeat(np.arange(D), K - 1); kk = np.tile(k, D)
    order = np.argsort(t, kind="stable")            # visit them in increasing t
    ip = 0.5 * a.sum() + np.cumsum(a[dim[order]])   # <y, |o'|> after each step
    n2 = 0.25 * D + np.cumsum(2 * kk[order])        # ||y||^2 grows by 2k
    cos = np.concatenate([[np.sqrt(D) * a.mean()], ip / np.sqrt(n2)])
    best = cos.argmax()                             # index 0 means t = 0
    tmax = 0.0 if best == 0 else t[order[best - 1]]
    y = np.clip(np.floor(tmax * a) + 0.5, 0.5, K - 0.5)   # round t |o'| to the grid
    code = np.where(op > 0, K - 0.5 + y, K - 0.5 - y).astype(np.uint8)
    return code, cos[best]
blocks.caption: Run on the toy o' it returns 1,1,1,0,0,1,1,0 at B = 1 (cosine 0.873), 2,3,3,1,1,2,3,0 at B = 2 (0.986), 5,6,7,3,3,4,7,0 at B = 3 (0.995) and 11,13,15,6,6,9,14,1 at B = 4 (0.9995).

blocks.md: A neat property: the most significant bit of each $B$-bit code is exactly the sign bit, because values from $2^{B-1}$ up are the positive half of the grid. So the 1-bit RaBitQ code is embedded inside every extended code, and $\langle \bar o, q\rangle$ is computed from the integer codes as $\frac{1}{\|\bar y\|}\left(\langle \bar y_u, q'\rangle - \frac{2^B - 1}{2}\sum_i q'[i]\right)$, an integer-weighted dot product like lesson 5's.

With B = 3, each coordinate maps to an integer 0 to 7 (grid values -3.5 to 3.5, shifted by 3.5). The search over t found 5,6,7,3,3,4,7,0, with <o-bar,o> = 0.995.
Values 4 to 7 are the positive grid points, so the top bit is the sign: 11100110, identical to the 1-bit code. The toy estimate improves from 0.607 to 0.719 (true 0.688).

blocks.md: The paper stores the top bits separately. At query time it first estimates every candidate from the top bits alone with the fast 1-bit path, drops candidates the bound rules out, and reads the remaining bits only for survivors. It proves the bits needed are asymptotically optimal and gives an empirical formula: with over 99.9% probability the inner-product error is below $2^{-B} \cdot 5.75/\sqrt{D}$. In its experiments $B = 5$ (about 6.4x compression) stably gave over 95% recall and $B = 7$ (about 4.5x) over 99%, without re-ranking on raw vectors.

blocks.title: Extended RaBitQ empirical error bound vs bits per dimension

scenes.caption: At D = 1024 the bound is 0.090 for B = 1 and halves with every extra bit: 0.0056 at B = 5 and 0.0014 at B = 7. The formula is fitted from the paper's experiments, not a theorem.
At D = 128 every value is sqrt(8) = 2.83x larger: low-dimensional vectors need more bits per dimension for the same accuracy.
At D = 3072 the curve drops by another 1.73x relative to 1024. Each extra bit buys a 2x reduction, while 1/sqrt(D) gains come only from more dimensions.

blocks.prompt: On the toy, a shortcut with no search (scale o' so its largest coordinate lands on the top grid level, then round) happens to give the same codes as the search. Will that shortcut, or plain scalar quantization, match the search for 768-dimensional vectors at B = 2?
blocks.reveal: **No.** In a simulation with 300 random 768-dimensional unit vectors (standing in for rotated embeddings), the mean cosine between the quantized and original vector at $B = 2$ was **0.939** for the search, **0.846** for the max-scaling shortcut and **0.856** for per-vector min/max scalar quantization. One outlying coordinate sets the scale for the shortcut and wastes most grid levels; the search finds a scale that balances all $D$ coordinates.

blocks.md: **Against plain scalar quantization.** The paper's closest baselines are SQ (one global range $[v_l, v_r]$ split into $2^B - 1$ steps) and LVQ (the same per vector, using each vector's own range). Both round each coordinate independently and use $\langle \hat o, q\rangle$ directly, without the search or the $\langle \bar o, o\rangle$ correction. In the same 768-dimensional simulation, with a near neighbor at true $\langle o, q\rangle = 0.7$, the mean absolute inner-product error was 0.0076 for extended RaBitQ against 0.0235 for per-vector min/max SQ at $B = 2$, 0.0043 against 0.0072 at $B = 3$, and 0.0021 against 0.0034 at $B = 4$. The gap shrinks as bits grow, matching the paper, which finds LVQ's error 1.3x to 3.1x larger at $B > 6$ and orders of magnitude larger at $B = 1$ or 2.

Extended RaBitQ only (SQ bars hidden): its largest single error over the 300 vectors was 0.0247, 0.0142 and 0.0071, under the paper's 99.9% formula 2^-B x 5.75 / sqrt(768) = 0.0519, 0.0259 and 0.0130.

blocks.md: Extended RaBitQ = a symmetric B-bit grid, normalized and randomly rotated. Encoding searches over a rescaling factor t, but only at the finitely many critical values where a coordinate's rounding changes. The same estimator, factor and bound carry over, and the top bits are the 1-bit code.

blocks.question: Why does the extended RaBitQ encoder only need to try finitely many rescaling factors t?
options: Because t must be an integer
Because the paper fixes t = 2^B for every vector
Because only the largest coordinate of o' depends on t
Because the rounded vector, and so its cosine with o', changes only when some t |o'_i| crosses a rounding boundary, at t = k / |o'_i|
blocks.explain: Rounding is piecewise constant: between two critical values no coordinate changes its rounded value, so the code and its cosine stay fixed. Checking each critical value once, in sorted order, covers every code that rounding t o' can produce, and Lemma 3.1 says the best code is among them.

blocks.question: An extended RaBitQ index stores 7-bit codes. Why does storing the most significant bits in a separate array speed up search?
options: The top bits form the 1-bit RaBitQ code, so a fast 1-bit estimate plus its bound can prune most candidates before the remaining 6 bits are read
It lets the index skip the random rotation
The most significant bits never change between queries
It halves the storage
blocks.explain: The top bit of each dimension equals the sign code. A cheap first pass on those bits, with the error bound, discards candidates that cannot qualify, and only survivors pay for the full-precision estimate.

blocks.md:
**In real systems** (as their docs describe today). The previous lessons give the vocabulary to read these docs: which centroid, whether there is a rotation, how many query bits.

- **Faiss** has `IndexRaBitQ` and `IndexIVFRaBitQ`, with an `nb_bits` option for multi-bit codes and a query-bits setting `qb` that defaults to 4. The index factory accepts strings such as `IVF4096,RaBitQ` or `RaBitQ4`, and a `RaBitQfs` FastScan variant. Its quantizer assumes the random rotation is performed externally, so add the `RR` (random rotation) prefix, as in `RR768,RaBitQ`.
- **Weaviate** offers rotational quantization (RQ) at 8, 4 and 1 bits. Its docs say RQ is inspired by extended RaBitQ but uses fast pseudorandom rotations; 1-bit RQ stores data signs and quantizes queries to 5 bits, and works on datasets like SIFT where BQ performs poorly. It also has plain BQ and over-fetches then rescores.
- **Qdrant** offers 1, 1.5 and 2-bit binary quantization with an optional scalar-quantized query, `oversampling` and `rescore`, and (v1.18+) TurboQuant: a fast random rotation, then 1 to 8 bits.

**Lucene and Elasticsearch: BBQ.** Better Binary Quantization arrived in Elasticsearch 8.16 and Lucene, and its authors say it was developed from RaBitQ's insights. Like RaBitQ it centers vectors on a centroid, stores the sign bits plus a few float correction values per vector (2 for Euclidean distance, 3 for dot product), quantizes the query to int4 and computes the bits-by-integers dot product with the same bit-plane AND plus popcount trick as lesson 5. The blog lists the differences: **one centroid** per segment (incrementally computed, re-averaged when segments merge) for simple HNSW integration, **no random rotation**, so the estimator is not unbiased over repeated runs, and rescoring that does not use the estimated error. You enable it with the `bbq_hnsw` or `bbq_flat` index type. This is BBQ as its 2024 launch blog describes it; Elastic later refined the format with optimized scalar quantization (OSQ).

That contrast shows which ingredient carries which property. **Centering** fixes the all-ones failure of plain sign bits. The **correction factors** and the **asymmetric query** recover most of the accuracy. The **random rotation** is what makes the error distribution identical for every input direction, which is what the unbiasedness and the bound need. Without it, BBQ relies on oversampling and rescoring with raw floats instead of a bound; its blog reports above 90% recall on 1M CohereV3 1024-dimensional vectors with 3x oversampling and HNSW, with the index taking 208 MB against 4,162 MB raw.

**Choosing, as a checklist.**

- High-dimensional, centered embeddings, raw vectors available for rescoring, simplest code: **plain BQ** with oversampling.
- Skewed or non-centered data, low dimensions, or you want an error bound: **1-bit RaBitQ** (centroid, rotation, two floats), for example Faiss `RR,RaBitQ` or Weaviate 1-bit RQ. On a Lucene stack, **BBQ** gives the centering and corrections without the rotation.
- Raw vectors cannot be kept for rescoring and you need over 95% recall: **extended RaBitQ at about 5 bits**. (Weaviate reports 98 to 99% recall from compressed distances alone for its 8-bit RQ, but only about 94 to 95% for 4-bit RQ, which leans on rescoring.)
- 4x compression is enough and you want about 99% without a second stage: **int8** scalar quantization.
- Frequent inserts: RaBitQ's codebook does not depend on the data, so new vectors encode without retraining, while PQ must train k-means codebooks (lesson 9 times both).

Choosing: plain BQ is simplest and fastest when embeddings are high-dimensional and centered, and you can afford rescoring. RaBitQ-style rotation plus correction factors costs a few bytes per vector and makes 1-bit codes robust on skewed data; BBQ keeps the centering and corrections but not the rotation. Multi-bit (extended RaBitQ, 8-bit RQ) is the route when you want to drop raw vectors from RAM entirely.

blocks.question: You must serve 1536-dimensional embeddings with over 95% recall and cannot keep float vectors anywhere (no RAM, no disk) for rescoring. Which option fits best?
options: 1-bit binary quantization with oversampling 8
Plain BQ with a Hamming-only ranking
1-bit RaBitQ with error-bound re-ranking
Extended RaBitQ with about 5 bits per dimension
blocks.explain: Every 1-bit option relies on re-ranking with stored originals to reach high recall. Extended RaBitQ was designed for this case: the paper reports B = 5 stably gives over 95% recall without raw-vector re-ranking.

blocks.question: Elasticsearch's BBQ centers vectors, stores correction values and uses an int4 query, but skips the random rotation. What does it give up compared with RaBitQ?
options: The 32x memory saving, since BBQ stores floats per dimension
The asymmetric query, since int4 queries cannot be used with bits
The guarantee that the estimator is unbiased with an error bound that holds for any data, so it relies on oversampling and rescoring instead
The ability to use HNSW
blocks.explain: The rotation makes the quantization error's distribution the same for every vector direction; the unbiasedness proof and the 1/sqrt(D) bound depend on it. BBQ's blog says that without rotating it does not have the unbiasedness property, and its rescoring does not depend on an estimated error. It still stores 1 bit per dimension and integrates with HNSW.

lessons.title: Build it: RaBitQ versus PQ and plain BQ on real embeddings

blocks.md: Time to run everything. Two datasets, chosen to match other courses so the numbers can be compared. **SciFact**: 5,183 abstracts and 300 claims embedded with nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (768 dimensions, layer norm then unit length). **SIFT10K**: 10,000 128-dimensional SIFT descriptors and 100 queries, with the same setup as the *Vector search and ANN* course; 77% of its coordinates are positive, against 49.9% for SciFact. Ground truth is the exact top 10; on unit vectors, Euclidean order is cosine order. Quality is **recall@10**, and oversampling $o$ means fetching $10 \cdot o$ candidates and rescoring them with the float vectors. One run on one laptop CPU with 2 threads.

blocks.code:
class RaBitQ:
    def __init__(self, X, seed=0):
        self.D = D = X.shape[1]
        self.c = X.mean(0)                              # global centroid
        G = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal((D, D))
        Q, R = np.linalg.qr(G)
        self.P = Q * np.sign(np.diag(R))                # random rotation
        r = X - self.c
        self.norm = np.linalg.norm(r, axis=1)           # float 1: ||o_r - c||
        op = (r / self.norm[:, None]) @ self.P          # o' = P^-1 o, row form
        self.bits = op > 0                              # the D-bit code
        self.f = np.abs(op).sum(1) / np.sqrt(D)         # float 2: <o-bar, o>

    def estimate(self, q, eps0=1.9):
        qc = q - self.c; qn = np.linalg.norm(qc)
        qp = (qc / qn) @ self.P                         # q' = P^-1 q
        xbar = np.where(self.bits, 1.0, -1.0) / np.sqrt(self.D)
        ip = (xbar @ qp) / self.f                       # unbiased <o, q>
        d2 = self.norm**2 + qn**2 - 2 * self.norm * qn * ip   # equation (2)
        err = np.sqrt(1 - self.f**2) / self.f * eps0 / np.sqrt(self.D - 1)
        return d2, d2 - 2 * self.norm * qn * err        # estimate, lower bound

def search(idx, X, q, k=10):
    est, lb = idx.estimate(q)
    top, n_exact = [], 0
    for i in np.argsort(est):
        if len(top) == k and lb[i] >= top[-1][0]:
            continue                                    # cannot enter the top k
        n_exact += 1
        top = sorted(top + [(((X[i] - q) ** 2).sum(), i)])[:k]
    return [i for _, i in top], n_exact

blocks.md: Every line maps to a lesson: the centroid and norm to lesson 3's step 1, the QR rotation (with the sign fix that makes it uniformly random) to step 3, `bits` and `f` to the stored code and factor, `ip` to lesson 4's estimator and `lb` to the bound. `search` is lesson 5's re-ranking extended from the single nearest neighbor to the top $k$: a candidate gets an exact distance only if its lower bound beats the current $k$-th best. With rotation seed 0, ranking by its estimate and rescoring gave recall@10 of 0.531, 0.72 and 0.887 at oversampling 1, 2 and 4 on SIFT10K, and 0.766, 0.936 and 0.989 on SciFact, close to Faiss below.

blocks.md: Read the PQ comparison carefully. PQ here uses 8-bit sub-codebooks (256 centroids per slice), which is accurate but needs table lookups in memory; the RaBitQ paper compared against fast-scan PQ with 4-bit codes and on speed at equal accuracy, not recall at equal bytes. What this run does show: PQ had to train. On this laptop, building PQ96x8 took **110.7 s** on SciFact and PQ16x8 **17.5 s** on SIFT10K (a rerun took 123 s and 20 s; wall times vary with machine and load) (k-means per slice, and Faiss warned that 5,183 training points is fewer than it wants), while 1-bit RaBitQ built in under 0.1 s (4-bit: 0.2 s): a mean and a rotation, no training. Per-query times at this tiny scale are fractions of a millisecond for every method and say little.

blocks.prompt: Faiss's RaBitQ quantizer assumes the rotation is applied outside it. What happens to recall@10 on SIFT10K if you build with the factory string "RaBitQ" instead of "RR128,RaBitQ"?
blocks.reveal: It drops from **0.55 to 0.424** at oversampling 1, and from 0.899 to 0.779 at oversampling 4. On SciFact the change is within noise (0.749 with the rotation, 0.759 without). SIFT's centered coordinates have very unequal spreads (per-dimension standard deviation from 16.5 to 53.1, against a 1.8x range on SciFact), and one sign bit per axis treats every axis alike. Without a rotation the mean stored factor falls to 0.764 instead of about 0.80: lesson 3's point that a fixed codebook favors some directions. It still beats centered sign bits (0.331), because the float query and the per-vector factor are still there.

blocks.md:
**Bound-based re-ranking instead of a fixed oversampling.** The numpy `search` with $\epsilon_0 = 1.9$ reached recall@10 of **1.0** on SIFT10K while computing on average 254.6 exact distances per query (2.5% of the 10,000 vectors), and **0.995** on SciFact with 41.2 exact distances (0.8% of 5,183). No oversampling factor was tuned; easy queries stop early and hard ones check more.

**IVF with per-cluster centroids** (Faiss `RR,IVF64,RaBitQ`, 64 lists). On SIFT10K with `nprobe = 16`, recall@10 was 0.685 at oversampling 1, above the 0.55 of one global centroid, and 0.987 at oversampling 4. On SciFact, `nprobe = 16` gave 0.756 and 0.929, but `nprobe = 4` gave 0.635 and 0.712: rescoring cannot recover neighbors that sit in lists you never probed.

**A sanity checklist before trusting your own numbers.**

1. **Unbiasedness.** Re-encode with 20 rotation seeds and average the estimate for fixed pairs. For five SciFact query and nearest-neighbor pairs, true inner products 0.379, 0.482, 0.312, 0.516, 0.585 averaged to 0.376, 0.478, 0.320, 0.516, 0.581 (seed-to-seed spread about 0.02 to 0.03).
2. **Bound coverage.** Check that the lower bound sits below the exact distance for the true neighbors: 98.0% of true top-10 neighbors on SciFact and 99.9% on SIFT10K.
3. **Metric.** For cosine, normalize vectors first. Faiss's quantizer stores metric-dependent factors, so build it with the metric you will query with; inner product goes through equation (2).
4. **Bytes.** Count the factors: 1-bit RaBitQ at 768 dimensions is 96 bytes of bits plus 8 of floats.

These are single runs on small datasets (5,183 and 10,000 vectors) on one machine. They show the mechanisms; for a decision, rerun on a sample of your own data at your own scale, since recall and speed rankings change with dimension, data skew and index size.

Measured here: plain sign bits fail on non-negative data (0.155 recall@10), RaBitQ's centering, rotation and factors fix that (0.55, or 0.899 with 4x oversampling), byte-matched PQ is competitive but needs training, and 4-bit extended RaBitQ reaches 0.91 to 0.96 without any rescoring.

blocks.question: On SIFT10K, plain sign-at-zero BQ gets recall@10 of 0.155 while 1-bit RaBitQ gets 0.55 at a similar size. Which RaBitQ step does most to explain the gap?
options: The 4-bit query quantization
Padding the code to a multiple of 64 bits
Storing the norm as a float
Subtracting the centroid before taking signs
blocks.explain: 77% of SIFT coordinates are positive, so sign-at-zero bits are mostly 1 and carry little information. Centering alone lifts BQ to 0.331 (the Vector search course's number). The rotation adds more (0.424 without it, 0.55 with it), and the float query and factor do the rest. The 4-bit query only saves time.

blocks.question: Your IVF-RaBitQ index has low recall at nprobe = 4. You raise oversampling from 1 to 4 and recall barely moves (0.635 to 0.712 on SciFact). What is the better next step?
options: Raise nprobe, since the missing neighbors are in clusters that were never scanned
Switch to a dense rotation matrix
Raise oversampling to 16
Lower the query bits from 4 to 2
blocks.explain: Rescoring only re-orders candidates from probed lists. At nprobe = 16 the same index reached 0.929 with oversampling 4. Oversampling fixes estimation error; nprobe fixes coverage.
